hello.title: Hello, Delphi!
hello.summary: Write your first Delphi console program and print text and numbers with Write and Writeln.
hello.lesson.0: Delphi is a tool for writing programs in the language **Object Pascal**. A Delphi program starts with the word `program` and a name. Its main part is a block between `begin` and `end.`, and the computer runs the lines in this block from top to bottom.
hello.lesson.2: Line by line: `program Hello;` gives the program a name. `{$APPTYPE CONSOLE}` is a **compiler directive**: it tells Delphi to build a console program, which writes text into a terminal window. `Writeln` writes the text inside the parentheses `( )` and then ends the line. The program ends with `end` and a period `.`.
hello.lesson.4: Each instruction is a **statement**. A semicolon `;` separates two statements. Text goes in single quotes, like `'Hi'`. Delphi does not care about upper or lower case in names: `Writeln`, `WriteLn` and `WRITELN` are the same.
hello.lesson.7: `Write` writes without ending the line. If you give `Writeln` several values, separated by commas, it writes them one after the other with no space between them. `Writeln` without values writes an empty line. Numbers have no quotes, so Delphi can calculate with them: `+` adds and `*` multiplies.
hello.lesson.9: To put a single quote inside a text, write it twice. `'It''s'` is the text `It's`. Inside quotes, `2 + 3` is only text, so Delphi does not calculate it.
hello.lesson.11: Text between `{` and `}` or after `//` is a **comment**, and Delphi ignores it. `{$` is special: `{$APPTYPE CONSOLE}` is not a comment but an instruction for the compiler.
hello.lesson.12: The last `end` of the program needs a period, not a semicolon. Text uses single quotes `'`, never double quotes `"`.
hello.card.0: `program Name;` + `{$APPTYPE CONSOLE}` start a console program
hello.card.2: `Writeln('Hi')` writes a line, `Write` stays on the line
hello-1.prompt: Which statement writes Hello and then ends the line?
hello-1.explain: `Writeln` ends the line, `Write` does not. Text goes in single quotes.
hello-2.explain: `4 + 5` has no quotes, so Delphi calculates `9` and writes it right after the text.
hello-3.explain: `Write` does not end the line, so `phi` follows directly after `Del`.
hello-4.statement: Delphi treats `Writeln` and `writeln` as the same name.
hello-4.explain: Delphi does not care about upper or lower case in names.
hello-5.prompt: Complete the code so that it compiles.
hello-6.explain: The main block of a program ends with `end` and a period.
hello-7.prompt: Build the statement that writes Total: 10.
hello-7.explain: `Writeln` takes the text in single quotes and the number, separated by a comma.
hello-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program writes Good morning on one line.
hello-8.explain: The statements go between `begin` and `end.`. `Write` comes first because it stays on the line.

variables.title: Variables and types
variables.summary: Store values in variables with var and const, and meet Integer, Double, string, Boolean and Char.
variables.lesson.0: A **variable** is a named place for a value. In Delphi you declare every variable before `begin`, in a `var` section. You write the name, a colon `:` and the **type**. The type says what kind of value the variable can hold.
variables.lesson.2: `:=` is the **assignment** operator: it stores the value on the right in the variable on the left. `Age := Age + 1` reads the old value, adds 1 and stores the result. A single `=` compares two values; it does not assign.
variables.lesson.4: `Integer` holds whole numbers and `Double` holds numbers with a decimal point. `string` holds text, `Boolean` holds `True` or `False`, and `Char` holds exactly one character, written in single quotes like `'A'`. You can declare several variables of the same type in one line: `A, B: Integer`.
variables.lesson.6: `Writeln(Price:0:2)` writes a `Double` with exactly 2 digits after the decimal point. The first number is the minimum width, and `0` means as wide as needed. Without this format, Delphi writes a `Double` in a long scientific notation with an `E`.
variables.lesson.8: `/` always gives a `Double`, even for two whole numbers. For whole-number division, use `div`. `mod` gives the remainder of that division.
variables.lesson.11: A **constant** never changes. Declare it in a `const` section with `=` instead of `:=`. Delphi takes the type from the value. If you try to assign a new value to a constant, the program does not compile.
variables.lesson.13: Delphi is **strongly typed**: every variable keeps its type. You cannot store a text in an `Integer` variable, and `Count := 2.5` does not compile when `Count` is an `Integer`. Names are not case sensitive: `age` and `Age` are the same variable.
variables.card.0: `var Age: Integer;` declares a variable before `begin`
variables.card.4: `div` and `mod` for whole numbers, `/` gives a `Double`
variables-1.prompt: Which line in a `var` section declares a variable for whole numbers?

variables-3.explain: `23 div 4` is `5`, because 4 fits 5 times into 23. The remainder is `3`.

strings.title: Strings
strings.summary: Join text with +, measure it with Length, and search, cut and change it with Pos, Copy, UpperCase and Format.
strings.lesson.0: A `string` holds a text of any length. The `+` operator joins two strings into a new one. This is called **concatenation**.
strings.lesson.2: `Length(S)` returns the number of characters in `S`. Square brackets read one character: `S[1]` is the first character, because Delphi strings start counting at 1. One character has the type `Char`.
strings.lesson.5: The unit `SysUtils` contains many helpers. To use it, add `uses SysUtils;` after `{$APPTYPE CONSOLE}`. `UpperCase` and `LowerCase` change the case of the letters, and `Trim` removes spaces at both ends. `IntToStr` turns a number into a string, so you can join it with `+`.
strings.lesson.8: `Pos(Sub, S)` returns the position where `Sub` first appears in `S`, or `0` if it is not there. `Copy(S, Start, Count)` returns `Count` characters of `S`, starting at position `Start`. If `Count` goes past the end, `Copy` stops at the last character.
strings.lesson.11: `Format` from `SysUtils` builds a string from a pattern and a list of values in square brackets. Each placeholder is replaced by the next value: `%s` for a string and `%d` for an integer.
strings.lesson.13: `+` only joins strings. `'Age: ' + 36` does not compile; write `'Age: ' + IntToStr(36)` instead. Inside `Writeln` you can also use commas: `Writeln('Age: ', 36)`.
strings-1.explain: `Length` counts every character, and the space counts too: 5 + 1 + 5 = 11.
strings-2.explain: Position 4 is the `b`. From there, `Copy` takes 5 characters: `board`.
strings-3.explain: `Pos` returns the first position. In `banana`, the first `a` is the second character.
strings-4.statement: In Delphi, `S[0]` is the first character of the string `S`.
strings-4.explain: Delphi strings start counting at 1, so the first character is `S[1]`.

strings-12.explain: `S + S` is `HiHi`, which has 4 characters. `UpperCase` gives `HIHI`, and `IntToStr` adds `4`.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Let your program choose with if, then and else, combine conditions with and, or and not, and pick a branch with case.
conditions.lesson.0: A program can make decisions. `if Condition then Statement` runs the statement only when the condition is `True`. A condition is a `Boolean` expression, for example a comparison.
conditions.lesson.2: The comparison operators are `=` (equal), `<>` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`. Remember: Delphi uses a single `=` to compare and `:=` to assign.
conditions.lesson.4: `else` gives a second path for the case that the condition is `False`. If a path needs more than one statement, put the statements in a `begin ... end` block.
conditions.lesson.6: To test several conditions one after the other, write `else if`: `if Score >= 90 then ... else if Score >= 70 then ... else ...`. Delphi checks them from top to bottom and runs only the first branch whose condition is `True`.
conditions.lesson.7: Never put a semicolon before `else`. The semicolon ends the whole `if` statement, so the `else` that follows has no `if`, and the program does not compile.
conditions.lesson.9: `and` is `True` when both sides are `True`. `or` is `True` when at least one side is `True`, and `not` turns `True` into `False` and back. Put each comparison in parentheses, like `(Age >= 13) and (Age <= 19)`. Without them, Delphi reads `and` first and the code does not compile.
conditions.lesson.12: `case` picks one branch by the value of an **ordinal** expression, which is a type with countable values, such as `Integer` or `Char`. Each branch has one or more values or a range like `1..5`, then a colon. `else` catches all other values. `case` does not work with strings.
conditions-1.explain: `7 mod 2` is `1`, so the condition is `False` and the `else` branch runs.
conditions-3.explain: `4` is in the range `3..5`, so the second branch runs.
conditions-4.statement: `if A > 0 and B > 0 then` is valid Delphi code.
conditions-4.explain: Delphi reads `0 and B` first. Write `if (A > 0) and (B > 0) then`.

conditions-12.explain: `A and B` is `False`, but `not B` is `True`. `False or True` is `True`.
loops.title: Loops
loops.summary: Repeat code with for to and downto, while and repeat until, and visit every element of an array with for in.
loops.lesson.0: A **loop** repeats code. The `for` loop counts: `for I := 1 to 3 do` runs its statement with `I` set to 1, 2 and 3. The counter is a variable that you declare yourself, usually an `Integer`. With `downto`, the loop counts backwards.
loops.lesson.2: If the start value is already past the end value, the body does not run at all. When the body has more than one statement, put them in a `begin ... end` block.
loops.lesson.5: `while Condition do` checks the condition **before** each round and repeats while it is `True`. Make sure that the body changes something in the condition, or the loop never ends.
loops.lesson.7: `repeat ... until Condition` checks the condition **after** each round, so the body always runs at least once. The loop stops as soon as the condition is `True`. It needs no `begin ... end`, even for several statements.
loops.lesson.10: An **array** is a list of values of the same type. `Names: array of string` declares one, and `Names := ['Ada', 'Bob', 'Cy']` fills it. `for Name in Names do` visits every element, one after another, without a counter. The unit about arrays shows more.
loops.lesson.12: `Break` leaves a loop at once, and `Continue` jumps to the next round.
loops.lesson.13: Do not change the counter of a `for` loop inside the loop; Delphi does not allow it. After the loop, the value of the counter is undefined, so do not use it there.
loops.card.0: `for I := 1 to 5 do` / `for I := 5 downto 1 do`
loops.card.1: `while N > 0 do begin ... end;` checks first
loops.card.2: `repeat ... until N > 50;` runs at least once
loops.card.3: `for Name in Names do` visits every element
loops-2.explain: The loop runs for 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4 and 3, which is 8 rounds.

loops-4.explain: `repeat` checks its condition only after the body has run.

routines.title: Procedures and functions
routines.summary: Group code into procedures and functions, return values with Result, and pass parameters by value, var, const and out.
routines.lesson.0: A **procedure** is a named block of code that you can run as often as you like. You declare it above the main `begin` of the program. To run it, write its name. This is a **call**.
routines.lesson.2: **Parameters** pass values into a routine. You list them in parentheses, each with its type. A **function** also returns a value: its type comes after the colon, and you set the value by assigning it to `Result`.
routines.lesson.4: A routine can have its own `var` section, like `I` in `Greet`. These **local variables** exist only while the routine runs, and only the routine can see them.
routines.lesson.6: A normal parameter is a copy: changes inside the routine do not change the variable of the caller. A `var` parameter is the caller's variable itself, so the routine can change it. A `const` parameter cannot be changed inside the routine; use it for strings, because it avoids a copy.
routines.lesson.8: An `out` parameter is like `var`, but it only passes a value **out** of the routine, so the routine must set it. Use `out` when a routine gives back more than one value.
routines.lesson.11: Two routines can have the same name if their parameters differ. Mark each of them with the directive `overload`. Delphi then picks the one that fits the arguments of the call.
routines.lesson.13: A routine must be declared before you call it. Put procedures and functions above the main `begin` of the program, and above other routines that call them.
routines.card.2: `var` changes the caller's variable, `out` only returns a value
routines-2.explain: `A` and `B` are `var` parameters, so `Swap` changes `X` and `Y` themselves.
routines-3.options.2: Nothing, the code does not compile.

routines-4.explain: `Result` holds the value that the function returns.

routines-5.explain: An `out` parameter does not bring a value in; the routine sets it for the caller.

arrays.title: Arrays
arrays.summary: Store many values in static and dynamic arrays, size them with SetLength, and loop over them with Length, Low and High.
arrays.lesson.0: An **array** holds many values of the same type under one name. A **static array** has a fixed size that is part of its type: `array[1..3] of Integer` has three elements with the indexes 1, 2 and 3. You read and write an element with its index in square brackets.
arrays.lesson.2: `Low(A)` returns the first index of the array `A`, `High(A)` returns the last index, and `Length(A)` returns the number of elements. Use `Low` and `High` in `for` loops, so that the loop still works when the size changes.
arrays.lesson.4: The indexes of a static array can start at any number, for example at 0. A constant array lists its values in parentheses: `const Days: array[0..2] of string = ('Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed');`.
arrays.lesson.7: A **dynamic array** has no size in its type: `array of Integer`. `SetLength(A, 3)` gives it 3 elements, and a later `SetLength` can make it bigger or smaller while it keeps the existing values. A dynamic array always starts at index 0, so the last index is `Length(A) - 1`, which is the same as `High(A)`.
arrays.lesson.9: You can also fill a dynamic array in one step with square brackets: `Names := ['Ada', 'Bob']`. To add one element, make the array one element longer and store the value at the new last index.
arrays.lesson.11: A parameter like `const Values: array of Integer` is an **open array**. It accepts a static array, a dynamic array or a list in square brackets. Inside the routine, it always starts at index 0.
arrays.lesson.13: Never use an index outside the array. A dynamic array with 3 elements has the indexes 0, 1 and 2, so `A[3]` does not exist. Reading or writing there is a serious bug: the program may crash or use wrong data.
arrays.card.0: `array[1..5] of Integer` is static, with a fixed size
arrays.card.1: `array of Integer` + `SetLength(A, 3)` is dynamic, from index 0

classes.title: Classes
classes.summary: Define your own types with classes: fields, a constructor, methods and properties, and free objects when you are done.
classes.lesson.0: A **class** is a blueprint for objects. It bundles data, the **fields**, with the routines that work on this data, the **methods**. A method can be a procedure or a function. You declare a class in a `type` section, and by convention class names start with `T`.
classes.lesson.2: `TPerson.Create` creates a new object, an **instance** of the class, and the variable `P` refers to it. A dot gives you access to its fields and methods: `P.Name`, `P.Greet`. You write the body of a method below the class, with the class name in front: `procedure TPerson.Greet;`. Inside the method, the fields can be used directly by name.
classes.lesson.3: Delphi does not clean up objects for you. When you no longer need an object, call its method `Free`. Use `try ... finally`: the code after `finally` runs even when an error happens in the `try` part, so the object is always freed.
classes.lesson.5: A **constructor** sets up a new object. Declare it with `constructor Create(...)` and give it parameters for the starting values. Its first statement `inherited Create;` runs the basic setup that every object needs.
classes.lesson.8: Fields in a `private` section are meant only for the class itself; code in other units cannot see them. By convention, their names start with `F`. A **property** gives controlled access: `read` names where the value comes from, and `write` names where a new value goes. A property without `write` is read-only.
classes.lesson.10: `Balance` has only `read`, so `Acc.Balance := 100` does not compile. The only way to change the balance is `Deposit`, which ignores amounts that are not positive. This keeps the object in a valid state.
classes.lesson.11: A variable of a class type only refers to an object. Before `Create`, it refers to no object, and using it crashes the program. After `Free`, do not use the object again.
classes.card.0: `type TPerson = class ... end;` declares a class
classes.card.3: `property Age: Integer read FAge write FAge;`
classes.card.4: `try ... finally P.Free; end;` frees the object
